sentence: In your sky, the Sun and the full Moon look the same size.
claim: Seen from Earth, the Sun and the full Moon have nearly the same angular size (about half a degree; on average the Sun about 32.0′, the Moon about 31.1′).
source_title: Astronomy Picture of the Day, 1 August 2008 (NASA)
note: APOD (excerpt): 400 times the diameter, 400 times farther, the same angular size. The reviewer's correction: on average the Sun is slightly larger (annular eclipses outnumber total ones), so the line says 'look the same size', not 'no bigger'.

sentence: But one is about four hundred times wider, and four hundred times farther away.
claim: The Sun is about 400 times the Moon's diameter and about 400 times farther from Earth.
source_title: Astronomy Picture of the Day, 1 August 2008 (NASA)
note: Also NASA StarChild ('over 400 times the diameter'). Computed: 1,392,700 / 3,474.8 = 401; 149.6e6 / 384,400 = 389.

sentence: Line Earths up across the Sun's face: a hundred and nine.
claim: About 109 Earths would fit across the Sun's face.
source_title: How Big Is the Sun? (NASA Space Place)
note: Bible source (§7 #4). Stanford Solar Center: diameter 109 times Earth's.

sentence: Your whole world would fit inside one big sunspot.
claim: Many sunspots are as large as Earth or larger (most 1,500–50,000 km across; a 2024 sunspot was almost 14 times Earth's size).
note: Windows to the Universe (excerpt): most spots range from about 1,500 to 50,000 km, many as large as Earth (12,742 km). NASA SVS captions (2024): almost 14 times the size of Earth. 'One big sunspot'.

sentence: Nearly twenty-five centuries ago, in Athens, Anaxagoras said the Sun was a fiery stone, bigger than southern Greece.
claim: Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE), from Clazomenae, working in Athens in the mid-5th century BCE, described the Sun as a fiery mass (a red-hot stone or metal) larger than the Peloponnese, the southern peninsula of Greece.
note: 'Nearly twenty-five centuries ago': c. 450–430 BCE ≈ 2,455–2,475 years ago (the reviewer's fix: 'twenty-four' would be after his death). 'In Athens', not 'of Athens': he was from Clazomenae.

sentence: Calling it a stone, not a god, got him charged with impiety.
claim: Anaxagoras was charged with impiety in Athens for calling the Sun a red-hot mass (a stone or metal) rather than a god (Sotion, in Diogenes Laertius 2.12).
note: Diogenes Laertius (Perseus, via perseids.org): indicted by Cleon for impiety for declaring the Sun a mass of red-hot metal; Satyrus gives a different prosecutor and charges. The trial's details (and some scholars, its historicity) are debated; the line says only that he was charged.

claim: Anaxagoras's claim ('larger than the Peloponnese') is true: the Sun (1,392,700 km across) is far larger.
note: 'Larger than' is a lower bound, so it was right (the reviewer's framing). 26 Oct (script audit): 'He was right' sounded like it backed the stone idea (the Sun is hot plasma, not a stone); 'Bigger, yes' endorses only the size, which is what this claim supports.

sentence: Melt down one point three million Earths, and they'd fill it.
claim: About 1.3 million Earths would fit inside the Sun (by volume).
note: Bible source. Stanford Solar Center: volume 1.3 million times Earth's. 'Melt them down': by volume; whole spheres would pack fewer (about 830,000 at random close packing, 960,000 at the densest packing). The screen says 'by volume'.

sentence: Some are more than a thousand times wider.
claim: The largest known stars are more than 1,000 times wider than the Sun (e.g. VY Canis Majoris, about 1,400–2,000 solar radii; Stephenson 2-18, about 2,150).
note: Excerpt: Stephenson 2-18 has an estimated radius 2,150 times the Sun's (uncertain); UY Scuti revised to about 755. 'More than a thousand times wider' holds for the largest few. The 99.8% (now c18) of the solar system's mass moved to the end card's footnote (NASA, bible source).

sentence: Yet among the stars, it's no giant.
claim: The Sun is a main-sequence (dwarf) star, not a giant: the largest known stars are over 1,000 times wider. (It is not a typical size either: it is more massive than roughly 90–95% of the Milky Way's stars, most of which are red dwarfs.)
source_title: How Big Is the Sun? (NASA Space Place)
note: NASA Space Place calls it 'average-sized'; the reviewer notes that by count it outweighs about 90% of the Milky Way's stars, so the line says 'ordinary', not 'average'. 26 Oct (script audit): 'it's ordinary', set against size, implied the Sun is a typical size, a popular myth. Search excerpts this session: AMNH ('more massive than nearly 90% of stars', https://www.amnh.org/explore/ology/astronomy/what-do-you-know-about-stars2), Big Think ('more mass than 95% of all stars'), Discover ('three-fourths are red dwarfs').

sentence: Astronomers even file the Sun under dwarf stars.
claim: The Sun is classed as a G2V star; the 'V' (main sequence) is the dwarf luminosity class, and it is popularly called a yellow dwarf.
source_title: Is the sun really a dwarf star? (Live Science)
note: Excerpt: 'the sun is a G-type main-sequence star, specifically a G2V star. The "V" indicates that it is a dwarf'; the term is technical and does not mean small. Its light is white; 'yellow' is a misnomer (not said).

sentence: Out there, this is what ordinary looks like.
claim: Stars like the Sun are common; on the scale of stars, the Sun is ordinary.
source_title: How Big Is the Sun? (NASA Space Place)

sentence: Light time, across the Sun: about five seconds.
claim: The Sun's diameter is about 1.39 million km: light crosses it in about 4.6 seconds.
source_title: The Sun's Vital Statistics (Stanford Solar Center)

sentence: Sun to Earth: eight minutes, twenty seconds.
claim: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.
source_title: How long does it take light from the Sun to get to Earth? (Smithsonian, How Things Fly)

sentence: By a factor of about seven thousand.
claim: The Sun (1,392,700 km across) is about 7,000 times wider than the Peloponnese: about 5,600× its longest diagonal (about 250 km), about 6,300–6,500× its width (about 215–220 km north–south and east–west), and about 8,400× a circle of its area (21,550 km², 166 km across).
note: 26 Oct (script audit): 8,000 was the equal-area figure, the top of the range; a viewer hears 'wider' as edge to edge. Area 21,549.6 km² (Wikipedia, search excerpt this session). The widths are computed from approximate coordinates (Cape Tainaron 36.39°N to Rio 38.31°N ≈ 214 km; Kyllini 21.12°E to Cape Skyllaion 23.55°E at 37.6°N ≈ 214 km), not from a source: a person checks. The picture's ring grows from 200 km (≈ 7,000×) to the Sun's width.

sentence: Next: since this started, you've flown at least two thousand kilometers.
claim: Earth orbits the Sun at about 29.78 km/s, so in the roughly 70 seconds before the tease you have travelled more than 2,000 km with it.
note: Computed: 29.78 km/s × 70 s = 2,085 km ('at least two thousand'; Earth's spin and the Sun's motion add more, which episode 6 covers).

claim: Seen from Earth, the Sun and the full Moon have nearly the same angular size (about half a degree; on average the Sun about 32.0′, the Moon about 31.1′).
source_title: Astronomy Picture of the Day, 1 August 2008 (NASA)
note: The hook's 'twins': the Sun and the full Moon look the same size (c1).

sentence: (end-card footnote, not spoken) The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system.
claim: The Sun accounts for about 99.8 percent of the mass in the solar system.
source_title: It's Surprisingly Hard to Go to the Sun (NASA)
note: 26 Oct (script audit): the footnote had no claim of its own. Not spoken, so lint warns it is uncited and the post's generated source list leaves it out: add this source to the post by hand.

claim: By volume the Sun holds about 1.3 million Earths, more than a million (c7 says it in full).
note: 26 Oct (script audit): the question takes the million for granted, so it carries a claim; it was tagged {-}.
